title: Design a Graph for a Real Project

questions.prompt: A designer draws a graph, counts ten nodes, and reports a critical path of four waves. No script was run — they read it off the diagram. Why is that not yet a defensible number?
options: Diagrams cannot show waves, so the number is meaningless
The critical path is the longest chain of *blocking* edges; if any edge is a soft edge drawn as blocking, the human count is too high and must be recomputed
Four is correct as long as there are ten nodes
The widest wave is the critical path, so they counted the wrong thing
questions.explanation: A hand count silently assumes every edge blocks; the honest number comes from removing soft edges and recomputing. Option A is false — diagrams do show waves. Option C invents a node-count relationship that does not exist. Option D conflates width with depth.

questions.prompt: `graph.mjs` reports no collision and a widest wave of five. Later the run has two agents editing `package.json` at once. What did the graph model miss?
options: Nothing; the collision is a runner bug
A node's `writes` list was incomplete, so the busy-write check had no way to see the shared file
The widest wave should have been capped at one
The critical path was computed wrongly
questions.explanation: The busy-write check is only as good as the `writes` field on each node; a missing file makes a real collision invisible. Option A is tempting but the graph is the model — an incomplete model is the design error. Option C destroys all parallelism. Option D is a different number and does not cause a write collision.

questions.prompt: To shorten the critical path, a team wants to convert their only blocking edge into a soft one by agreeing an interface — but the interface would be a guess about a third-party API they cannot test yet. What is the right call?
options: Convert it anyway; fewer blocking edges is always better
Leave it blocking: an unverifiable interface is a bet whose reconciliation cost likely exceeds the wait
Delete the downstream node so the path shortens
Add a decision node to remove the edge automatically
questions.explanation: Conversion is a comparison of wait cost against reconciliation cost; an untestable interface is close to a guaranteed reconciliation. Option A is the tempting slogan this whole phase warns against. Option C removes work rather than restructuring the graph. Option D is a category error — a decision node records a choice, it does not delete a data dependency.

questions.prompt: A graph has a critical path of three waves and a widest wave of one. A colleague says the design is broken because it has zero parallelism. What is the honest reading?
options: The project is a true pipeline: every step needs the previous, so there is no parallelism to extract as decomposed — worth knowing before spending on agents
They must have missed soft edges, so mark three soft
Widest wave of one always means a cycle
questions.explanation: Width one with a real chain is a legitimate pipeline; the value is knowing it before paying for fan-out. Option A blames the tool. Option C is tempting because plans often over-block, but inventing soft edges without evidence is how you ship a collision. Option D is false — a cycle fails earlier, at the acyclic check, and would make the run impossible rather than narrow.
